rationale: B wins because it keeps the loaded word "default" under control and turns ambiguity into reporting work: "What does 'default' mean operationally" is the adult in the room. A has good bones, but "One coffee chain just made dairy optional. Dairy is taking notice" overstates the supplied fact and invents a reaction it does not have. B also finds the sharper defensive risk: "What happens to the workers when Oatly shuts the plant" is not pretty, but it is the story Oatly has to be ready for.
gaps_in_A: "One coffee chain just made dairy optional" is not supported. The update says default non-dairy option, not that dairy stopped being the default drink base.
"Dairy is taking notice" invents a reaction. The set later asks for a dairy source, which proves it does not have that fact yet.
"When oat milk stops being the alternative and becomes the default pour" repeats the same default-placement fact and risks the same overclaim unless additional category evidence exists.
A misses the labor/local-business defensive angle around the plant closure, even though that is the most likely ugly follow-up story.
gaps_in_B: "Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product" overclaims. The update only says this blend has a 31% lower footprint than its previous formula, not that it is Oatly's lowest-footprint product overall.
"evidence the user can cite for the green-premium belief" is a proof requirement the set does not already have; fine to request, but the angle weakens without it.
The no-price-change angle needs sharper separation between retail shelf price and foodservice pricing; the coffee-chain partnership does not automatically inherit the retail fact.
